**The Weight of a Single Word**

There’s a moment, just before dawn, when the world holds its breath. The air is thick with the kind of silence that isn’t absence but presence—an almost tangible thing, like the pause between heartbeats. I’ve always loved that moment. It feels like the universe is waiting for something, though I’ve never been sure what.

Maybe it’s waiting for a word.

Words are strange, aren’t they? They’re the building blocks of everything—stories, lies, love letters, wars. A single syllable can unravel a life or stitch one back together. I’ve seen it happen. A man once told me, *"I’m sorry,"* and the weight of those two words crushed him more than any fist ever could. Another time, a woman whispered *"stay,"* and suddenly the room was warmer, the air easier to breathe.

But words can also be empty. Hollow. Like the *"I love you"* said out of habit, or the *"everything will be fine"* spoken to soothe rather than believe. We throw them around like coins, not realizing how much they cost.

I wonder if that’s why some people stop speaking altogether. Not because they have nothing to say, but because they’re afraid of saying the wrong thing. Or worse—saying the right thing and having it mean nothing.

---

I used to keep a journal. Not the kind with pretty covers and lock-and-key, but a battered notebook with coffee stains and dog-eared pages. I’d write in it when the world felt too loud, when the noise of other people’s words drowned out my own. Sometimes I’d fill pages with rants—about politics, about heartbreak, about the way the sky looked like a bruise after a storm. Other times, I’d write one line and stare at it for hours, turning it over in my mind like a pebble in my palm.

*"What if the only thing that matters is the space between the words?"*

I never knew what that meant. Maybe it’s about the things we don’t say—the pauses, the hesitations, the way a person’s breath catches before they answer a question. Maybe the most honest conversations happen in the silence.

---

There’s a story my grandmother used to tell me. She said that in the old country, there was a village where people believed words had power. Not just the power to hurt or heal, but the power to *change*. If you spoke a wish into the wind at midnight, it would come true—but only if you truly meant it. The villagers were careful with their words. They didn’t lie, not even in jest. They didn’t gossip. They didn’t make promises they couldn’t keep.

One day, a traveler came through the village. He was a storyteller, and he told tales of distant lands where words were cheap, where people said whatever they wanted without thought. The villagers were horrified. *"How do you live like that?"* they asked. The traveler just laughed. *"How do you live like this?"*

My grandmother never told me how the story ended. Maybe because there is no ending. Maybe because the point was never about the traveler or the villagers, but about the choice we all have to make—whether to treat words like sacred things or like trash.

---

I’ve been thinking a lot about choices lately. Not the big ones—*Should I quit my job? Should I move across the country?*—but the small ones. The ones that slip by unnoticed. Like choosing to say *"thank you"* instead of *"I guess that’s fine."* Like choosing to listen instead of waiting for your turn to speak. Like choosing to write *"I miss you"* even if you’re not sure they’ll write back.

Words are the only magic we have left. And yet, we use them so carelessly.

---

I don’t know how to end this. Maybe because endings are just another kind of word—one we use to pretend things are finished when really, they’re just changing shape. So instead of an ending, I’ll leave you with a question:

*What’s the last word you spoke that you truly meant?*

And more importantly—*what’s the next one?*
